# R14 + R15 + R16 - companions: size by stakes, telemetry routing, roles (design for review, wave 25)

Goal: a panel takes as many companions as the stakes need, from as many labs as it can, chosen
by their track record with a share of exploration, and a companion can take a narrow role.
Today `-Panel` takes every available roster entry (weighty ones only on weighty purposes) in
roster order; selection is deterministic and telemetry (`-Rate`, the scoreboard) is only read
by humans.

## Code facts

- `Select-PanelMembers` (common.ps1) walks the roster: availability (preflight, endpoint health,
  peak), then `panel: weighty` vs the purpose (`$script:WeightyPurposes`), `-PanelAll`.
- Ratings live in `findings.json` `ratings[]` (`-Rate <n> -Useful yes|partly|no -Note`), joined
  to the ledger entry by n; `codex-scoreboard.ps1` aggregates per (lineage, purpose) across all
  tasks of the repository (`Read-AllTaskConsults` reads every ledger already, for endpoint
  health).
- Purposes: framing, decision, checkpoint, core-contract, acceptance, diff-review, stuck, chore
  (+ none); presets set effort and max words.

## Design

R14 - size and diversity
1. Default panel size per purpose: checkpoint 1, diff-review 2, framing 3, decision 3,
   core-contract 4, acceptance 4, stuck: all available. `-PanelSize <n>` overrides (n >= 1);
   `-PanelAll` = all available (unchanged). The size counts members that will RUN; skipped
   entries never count.
2. Lab diversity: optional roster field `lab` (free text, e.g. `deepseek`, `moonshot`, `zhipu`,
   `google`, `bytedance`, `alibaba`, `xiaomi`, `meta`, `openai`); default = the provider label.
   Filling a panel of size k: first one member per distinct lab (best-ranked of each lab), then
   the rest by rank. Validation: `lab` is a non-empty string.
3. The design floor is a rule, not code: the consult-codex skill states that framing and
   decision questions go to a panel of at least one companion (never only the author's own
   judgement), and `-Panel` on those purposes warns when fewer than 2 members will run.
4. Documented diminishing returns (README): past about five diverse members, findings repeat.

R15 - telemetry routing
5. Rank = a score per (roster entry, purpose[, topics]) from the ratings of the last 90 days
   across all tasks of the repository: score = 1 + sum(yes) + 0.5*sum(partly) - sum(no), floor
   0.25; a lineage with no ratings on this purpose scores its all-purpose score, else the
   neutral 1. Topics: `-Topic a,b` on the bridge (ledger `topics[]`, the scoreboard gains
   `-By topic`); a rating counts for the topics of its consultation; the score for a topic'd
   request = mean of the purpose score and the topic scores that exist.
6. Selection = weighted draw without replacement over the eligible entries (weights = scores),
   with exploration: with probability 0.2 per slot the slot is filled uniformly from the eligible
   rest. The RNG is seeded per panel (the panel id) and the ledger's `panel` object gains
   `routing: { seed, eligible: [{lineage, score, lab}], picked: [...], explored: [...] }`;
   the dry run prints the same. `-PanelOrder roster` restores today's deterministic order (and
   is the behaviour when no ratings exist at all: draw with equal weights = roster order? No -
   equal weights still shuffle; with no ratings the order is the roster order, documented).
7. Single runs (`-Provider` absent, no `-Panel`): today the first available roster entry. R15
   changes nothing there (the coordinator asked for one reviewer; the roster order is the
   coordinator's ranking).

R16 - roles
8. `-Role <name>`: a role block from `templates/role-<name>.md` appended to the prompt after
   the ask (edge-cases, security, tests, docs shipped; a repository may add its own under
   `.collab/roles/`), recorded as ledger `role`; `-Panel -Role x` gives the same role to every
   member; `-Roles a,b,c` (panel only) assigns roles in order to the picked members (the rest:
   none). Roles change the prompt only - members stay read-only, verdict rules unchanged.

## Tests (fakes only)

Sizes per purpose and `-PanelSize`; lab diversity (two entries of one lab, one of another:
size 2 picks one of each); the floor warning; scores from synthetic ratings (yes/partly/no,
the 90-day cut, the fallback chain); the seeded draw is reproducible (same seed -> same pick)
and exploration happens at the recorded rate over many seeds; `-PanelOrder roster`; the
ledger's routing record and the dry-run text; `-Topic` in the ledger and `-By topic`;
`-Role` block in the prompt and ledger, unknown role refused, `-Roles` assignment order.

## Questions for the reviewers

Q1. The score formula (additive, floor 0.25, 90-day window): sane, or should it be a rate (yes
    over rated) with a confidence prior (few ratings -> pull to neutral)?
Q2. Exploration 0.2 per slot: right order of magnitude for a roster of ~10 and a few panels a
    day? Any reason to make it decay with the number of ratings?
Q3. Diversity before rank: any case where it picks a clearly worse lab representative over a
    better second model of the same lab that the coordinator would regret?
Q4. Should a role change the purpose presets (effort, max words), or stay prompt-only?

## Addendum (2026-09-26, the maintainer's request): availability the operator can act on

The maintainer: the operator should see, briefly, which reviewers are out on a limit and until
when, because some topics should not be started without a particular reviewer.

9. Availability line, sharpened: the SessionStart hook line (and `codex-providers.ps1 -Short`,
   new) names only what is OUT, per roster entry (not per provider label), with the reset time
   in local time and a relative hint: `codex-consult: out - openai :: gpt-6-astra (until Sun
   20:35, 2d 10h), gemini :: * (until Sun 21:30); 9 of 11 reviewers available`. Every entry
   available: `codex-consult: all 11 reviewers available`. A quota failure WITHOUT a known reset
   (e.g. BytePlus 429 at 10:31 today, which the hook still reports as available) marks the
   endpoint "out (limit hit 10:31, reset unknown - retry after 60 min)" for 60 minutes.
10. `-Require <lineage[,lineage]>` on `-Panel` (and on a single run with `-Provider`): the run is
    refused BEFORE anything starts when a required reviewer is unavailable, printing who and
    until when, exit 5; the dry run shows the same. The roster may carry the default:
    `"require": { "acceptance": ["openai :: gpt-6-astra"], "framing": [...] }` per purpose.
11. The consult-codex skill: before a framing, decision, core-contract or acceptance panel the
    coordinator runs the availability check and, when a reviewer the topic needs is out, tells
    the operator who is out and until when and asks whether to wait or to proceed without them -
    never silently proceeds. The bridge's own summary already names skipped members; this rule
    moves the decision before the run.

Q5. Should "out" be judged per roster entry (two agy models share one quota - both out) or per
    endpoint group as `Get-PanelPlan` defines it, and how should the hook line stay one line with
    an 11-entry roster?

# Roadmap

Features the bridge should grow. Each entry names the problem it solves; the order is the
order we would build them. Agreed on 2026-09-23 between the Claude Code coordinator and the
Codex reviewer after a seven-wave implementation task with three consultations (framing,
acceptance, re-acceptance), and merged with the earlier help-wanted list.

## Review workflow

- **R1 â€” Core-contract checkpoint preset.** A review mode meant to run BEFORE dependent
  implementation starts (once the core interfaces, recovery and persistence paths exist) and to
  be re-triggered by changes to recovery, persistence or interfaces. Rationale: on the task that
  motivated this list every acceptance HOLD cost a full fix wave, because the core had been
  built on and the state-machine defects were found only at the end. Reviewing every mechanical
  wave is not the answer; reviewing contract boundaries is.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” `-Purpose core-contract` (xhigh effort, 900-word preset),
  narrowed by amendment to the interfaces and state machines named in the brief rather than
  the whole system, to fit the word budget.
- **R2 â€” Brief template.** A skeleton the coordinator fills for a checkpoint or acceptance:
  delta since the last review, the invariants claimed, changed files, unresolved findings,
  evidence paths, and the decision requested. Small critical executable files (a boot hook, an
  install script) go inline; everything else by exact path and revision. Rationale: a spec-only
  brief hid a one-character glob bug in a 100-line hook that a code reader would have seen.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” `templates/brief-framing.md` and `templates/brief-review.md`.
- **R3 â€” Structured findings companion.** Beside the Markdown reply, a machine-readable list
  (via Codex `--output-schema`, already on the help-wanted list): finding id, severity,
  file:line, claim, trigger, evidence level, verification step, proposed remedy. Rationale: the
  coordinator verifies every finding before acting; a parseable list makes that step and the
  later "verified" bookkeeping (see TECH_DEBT T1) mechanical. Structure is not proof; the
  verification step stays.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped**, revised beyond the original proposal after a design-review
  HOLD: `evidence` became an array of `{kind, reference, observation}` (what was already
  checked, not just a level), `locations[]` replaced a `"path:line"` string, and every reply
  is locally validated against the schema (see TECH_DEBT T1 status).
- **R4 â€” Acceptance output standard.** Every acceptance reply ends with four fixed blocks:
  verdict, blockers, unproven scenarios, and an OBSERVABLE first-run checklist (what must be
  in the logs before an exit code 0 is believed). Rationale: "what would justify acceptance?"
  was the most useful thing the reviewer produced, and it should not depend on being asked.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” the four blocks are rendered LAST in the reply file (after
  the verbatim prose, findings and prior findings), per the design-review amendment.
- **R5 â€” Review-purpose presets with measurements.** Presets for framing / checkpoint /
  acceptance / diff review with default effort levels, and a ledger record of effort, latency
  and the rework each review triggered. Rationale: a medium-effort checkpoint may be the right
  trade for quota, but today there is no comparison that proves it; measure first.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” the preset table plus `codex-findings.ps1 -Stats`, joining
  findings to the consultation that produced them via `source.consult`.
- **R6 â€” Role-split guidance.** Document primary (not exclusive) responsibilities when two
  reviewers exist: a fresh-context verifier of the same model family for mechanics (lint,
  interpreter compatibility, build, test wiring) and the Codex reviewer for protocol, state
  machines and "what the evidence does not show". Either may challenge anything. Rationale: on
  the motivating task the two found mostly different defects; together they were the coverage.
  **Status (0.2.0): shipped** â€” a "Role split" section in the skill and the README; no
  tooling enforces it, it is guidance for the coordinator.

Very important observations:

1. The rating is stored per-task in `findings.json` under `ratings[]`, keyed by `n` (the ledger number within the task). The lineage/provider/model/purpose are copied at rating time. Note: `lineage` for a rating of an entry from a legacy ledger is 'unknown provenance'.

2. Crucially: a rating's `n` is unique per TASK. Two tasks each have n=1. So `ratings[]` are per-task arrays — aggregating across all tasks requires reading every `findings.json` (the design says "across all tasks of the repository: `Read-AllTaskConsults` reads every ledger already, for endpoint health"). But `Read-AllTaskConsults` reads only `sessions.json` — NOT `findings.json`. So the design's claim ("Read-AllTaskConsults reads every ledger already") is true for ledgers but the RATINGS live in findings.json, which is a different file per task. So the scoring path needs a new all-task findings reader. That's a code fact error in the brief? Let's check: the brief says "Ratings live in findings.json ratings[] (-Rate ...), joined to the ledger entry by n; codex-scoreboard.ps1 aggregates per (lineage, purpose) across all tasks of the repository (Read-AllTaskConsults reads every ledger already, for endpoint health)." The scoreboard reads both — let me verify the scoreboard reads all findings.json files too. Yes: "Reads the ledgers (<CollabDir>/<task>/sessions.json) and findings stores (<CollabDir>/<task>/findings.json) of EVERY task of this repository". So the scoreboard has its own reader. But `Read-AllTaskConsults` in common.ps1 only reads sessions.json. The bridge (codex-consult.ps1) uses `Read-AllTaskConsults` for endpoint health. So implementing scoring in the bridge needs a new function to read all findings.json across tasks. This is a real gap: the parenthetical in the brief misleads — the ratings are NOT in the ledgers. Also important: the bridge's scoring would add a full read of every task's findings.json (which are large: 4097 lines etc.) on EVERY panel run — a performance concern. Let me check sizes.

Also, note the `when` field on ratings — the rating's own timestamp is when it was recorded, not when the consultation happened. The design says "the ratings of the last 90 days". Which timestamp? The rating's `when` (when the judge rated) vs the ledger entry's `when` (when the consultation ran). Using the rating's `when` means an old consultation rated recently counts. Also, re-rating replaces the record (keeping only the latest), so a rating's `when` gets refreshed on re-rate. That's a defect: the 90-day window is ambiguous and re-rating resets the clock, letting a stale signal persist. Also, ratings have no link to `lab` or to topics.

Another key defect: ratings are keyed by lineage string ('<provider> :: <model>' with engine suffix), but roster entries are (provider, model, engine). The design says "Rank = a score per (roster entry, purpose)". Joining a rating to a roster entry requires matching lineage → entry. Format-ReviewerLineage appends ' [engine]'. But two roster entries can share the same label with different models (fine). However: the same *model* under two different provider labels? Then lineages differ. More important: `-Provider` runs outside the roster produce lineages with no roster entry (the design says rank per roster entry). Also: an entry whose `model` is absent resolves to the config's model — the recorded lineage would be that resolved model, but roster entry has no Model; matching must go through resolution. Let me check Format-ReviewerLineage and how the ledger records reviewer.

Also: the ledger's `reviewer.provider` for the built-in openai. Let me check what happens with legacy entries: lineage 'unknown provenance'. Those ratings would be dropped or aggregated under a lineage that matches nothing → wasted signal.

3. Endpoint health: `Get-EndpointHealth` is per ENDPOINT (provider_fingerprint), not per roster entry. The addendum Q5 asks: should "out" be per roster entry or per endpoint group? Key code fact: `Get-EndpointHealth` keys on the fingerprint, and `Get-PreflightVerdict` uses that health for the entry. So two agy models sharing one Google sign-in share a fingerprint? Let me check `Resolve-ReviewerIdentity` for the agy engine — does the fingerprint include the model? If the fingerprint is per endpoint (base_url + wire_api), then two agy entries with different models have the SAME fingerprint → both out. Let me verify.

Also the addendum's "quota failure WITHOUT a known reset ... marks the endpoint 'out (limit hit 10:31, reset unknown - retry after 60 min)' for 60 minutes" — that's ALREADY implemented: the doc comment at line 4412-4414 says "Quota: the newest of {success, quota failure} is a quota failure that still blocks: its RetryAfter lies in the future, or it has no RetryAfter and is <= 60 min old". So item 9's "retry after 60 min" claim is already the behaviour — the addendum claims a gap ("BytePlus 429 at 10:31 today, which the hook still reports as available") that may be wrong. Let me check: the hook uses `-NoNetwork`, and health comes from THIS repository's ledgers. So if the BytePlus 429 was recorded in this repo's ledger within 60 minutes, the hook should already show it as unavailable (usage limit). The addendum's claim that "the hook still reports as available" needs verification. Let me look at the ledger for a byteplus 429 and the health logic. Note the "60 min" rule: if the failure is older than 60 min and has no RetryAfter, the endpoint is considered available again — so at "10:31 today" with the hook run later than 11:31, it'd read available. That's by design (documented). So the addendum's premise is partly wrong: the rule already exists; what's missing is only the *wording* ("reset unknown") and the fact it silently expires after 60 min. Let me verify Get-EndpointHealth's quota branch and QuotaKnown.

Let me read lines 4425-4570 fully.

4. `-Require`: need to check whether there's an existing refusal exit code 5 convention. Let me search for exit codes in codex-consult.ps1.

Let me check: Stop-WithError → exit code? And whether there's an existing exit code for "refused before start". Let's grep for 'exit 5' or exit codes.

5. The seeded draw: panel id as seed. Need to check what the "panel id" is and whether it's available at selection time. Let me look at Get-PanelPlan usage and the panel record in codex-consult.ps1. Search for 'panel_id' or `$panelId`.

Critical defect candidate: if the seed is derived from the panel id, and the panel id is deterministic per run (e.g. derived from consult ids or a timestamp), then the draw is reproducible only if the seed is recorded. The design records `seed` in the ledger — good. But: the eligibility set changes between the dry run and the real run (preflight is time-dependent; endpoint health changes), so the same seed with a different eligible list yields a different pick. Also, a `-DryRun` prints routing but the real run re-draws → the dry run is not a promise. That's a notable defect: seeded reproducibility is claimed ("the seeded draw is reproducible (same seed -> same pick)") but the eligible set is computed at run time from live health, so the recorded `picked` may not match the dry run.

Also: RNG determinism in PowerShell 5.1 vs 7 — `[Random]::new($seed)` is fine, but the weighted draw without replacement implementation must be specified; the design does not name the RNG algorithm (System.Random vs a hash-based PRNG). `[System.Random]` with the same seed gives the same sequence within a .NET version, but differs between .NET Framework 4.x (PS 5.1) and .NET 6+ (PS 7)? Actually System.Random(seed) is documented to produce the same sequence... In .NET Core 3.0+, `Random(Int32)` seeding algorithm changed (subtractive generator retained for seeded constructor — Microsoft documented that seeded Random remains the same algorithm for compatibility). Hmm, in .NET 6, `Random(seed)` still uses the Knuth subtractive algorithm, so the same sequence. But parameterless `Random()` changed. Still, it's worth flagging that the bridge must run on both PS 5.1 and PS 7 (a stated invariant in this repo), and cross-version reproducibility of the draw is not guaranteed unless the algorithm is pinned (e.g. an explicit xoshiro/splitmix or SHA-256-based derivation). That's a real defect for "the seeded draw is reproducible" test. Let me verify the repo's PS 5.1/7 dual-support claim (hook says "Runs on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7").

Also `Get-Sha256Hex` exists in common.ps1 — could be used for a portable PRNG.

6. Diversity: "first one member per distinct lab (best-ranked of each lab), then the rest by rank" conflicts with the weighted draw in item 6. Item 2 says filling uses "best-ranked of each lab, then the rest by rank" (deterministic rank order), while item 6 says selection is a weighted random draw with exploration. These two are contradictory: which governs? The design never says how diversity and the stochastic draw compose. That's a blocker-level ambiguity. E.g. does the draw happen within the lab-representative pass (draw the lab order? draw the lab's representative?), and does exploration override the diversity pass (an explored slot could take a second member of a lab already represented, defeating diversity)? Also: with `k >= number of distinct labs`, the "rest by rank" pass is unbounded.

Also: `lab` default = the provider label. But endpoint groups (Get-PanelPlan) merge labels that share a fingerprint — e.g. two agy labels ('gemini' and another agy label) share one Google sign-in, so they'd be ONE endpoint group but TWO labs by the default rule. Conversely byteplus hosts both `dola-seed-2.0-pro` and `kimi-k2.5` (from the ratings sample!) — one label 'byteplus' → default lab 'byteplus' → treated as ONE lab, though Kimi (Moonshot) and Dola (ByteDance) are different labs. So the default `lab` = provider label is actively wrong for the existing roster: it collapses ByteDance + Moonshot into one lab, and splits Google's agy entries. Let me verify the roster example file to confirm byteplus carries both kimi and dola.

7. Size vs concurrency: `Get-PanelPlan` computes the effective concurrency; a size-k panel of one endpoint group runs serially. Also, the panel size interacts with `-PanelConcurrency`/Cap: if Cap < k, the run takes longer. Not a defect per se, but sizing must consider that the members that RUN is only known after preflight, and a member can fail at launch (engine launch block). "The size counts members that will RUN; skipped entries never count" — but availability is evaluated at selection time; a member can still fail mid-run (a 429 during the run), so the actual number that produces a reply may be < k. There's no top-up/refill rule. Defect: no policy for "picked k, only j produced a usable reply" (no retry/top-up, and the design's floor rule for framing/decision counts members that WILL RUN, not members that DID).

8. Purpose default sizes: 'stuck: all available' but no default for `chore` and `none` (the '' purpose). The preset table has 8 purposes + none; the size table lists only 7 (checkpoint, diff-review, framing, decision, core-contract, acceptance, stuck) — missing `chore` and `none`/`''`. Defect: unspecified default size for chore and no-purpose runs → implementation must invent it. Also `chore` uses low effort and 400 words; a panel of 4 on a chore is a waste; and `none` is what the coordinator gets without -Purpose. Let me confirm the exact set: validPurposes = framing, decision, checkpoint, core-contract, acceptance, diff-review, stuck, chore. The size list omits chore and none. Confirmed defect.

9. Interaction with `panel: weighty`: the size table says framing 3, decision 3 — and weighty entries join only on weighty purposes. But `-PanelSize 4` on a *light* purpose (checkpoint/diff-review/chore) with a roster where most entries are weighty: the eligible pool may be smaller than k. The design doesn't say whether `-PanelSize` overrides the weighty gate (i.e. does a bigger size pull in weighty reviewers on a light purpose?). Also `-PanelAll` = all available (unchanged) — so `-PanelSize` and `-PanelAll` conflict; need mutual exclusion. Defect: unspecified interaction of -PanelSize with -PanelAll, -PanelConcurrency, weighty gate, and -Engine/-Model filters (which shrink the eligible set).

10. The `-PanelOrder roster` fallback: the design text itself contains an unresolved question inline: "with no ratings the order is the roster order, documented) — draw with equal weights = roster order? No - equal weights still shuffle". That's a self-contradiction in the spec (it edits itself mid-sentence). And it introduces a behavioural cliff: the moment the FIRST rating exists anywhere in the repo, the whole panel selection switches from deterministic roster order to a shuffle — a silent, non-obvious mode change that would break existing tests and the operator's expectations. Also, "no ratings exist at all" — globally, or no ratings for the eligible entries? Ambiguous.

11. Exploration 0.2 per slot with k slots: probability that at least one slot explores = 1 - 0.8^k; for k=4 that's 59%. Over a roster of ~10 with a few panels a day, the low-scoring entries get a lot of traffic; combined with the additive score with floor 0.25 and no confidence prior, a single "no" rating drives score to 0.25 vs neutral 1 — a 4x weight difference from ONE rating. Q1: yes, use a rate with a Beta prior (e.g. Wilson / Laplace), because additive scores are unbounded and length-biased: a lineage with 10 "yes" scores 11, one with 1 "yes" scores 2 — that's the intended, but a lineage with 100 consultations of which 90 yes/10 no scores 46 vs a lineage with 3 yes scoring 4 — fine. The real problem is variance: with few ratings the score is dominated by noise, and since the score also drives the *diversity* pass ("best-ranked of each lab"), one bad rating picks the lab's representative wrongly. Also, the additive formula never accounts for the number of consultations that were NOT rated (a lineage that ran 50 times and got 3 ratings looks neutral-ish 1+... while one that ran 3 times and got 3 ratings looks decisive). Also `no` = -1 and `partly` = +0.5 means a single 'no' can outweigh a 'yes'. And the floor 0.25 keeps a hated reviewer in the draw with weight 0.25 vs 11 — a 2% chance per slot; combined with 0.2 uniform exploration, the exploration dominates the floor anyway (uniform over eligible gives a hated entry 1/10 = 10% per explored slot), so the floor is nearly inert. That's a note: the floor and the exploration overlap; the exploration sets the real floor at ~2% (0.2 * 1/n).

Also: score is per (entry, purpose[, topics]) but ratings carry purpose only; the topic score requires the rating's consultation to have topics — the ledger `topics[]` is new (R15 adds `-Topic`). So for the first 90 days there are no topics at all → topic scores never exist → "mean of the purpose score and the topic scores that exist" degenerates to the purpose score. Fine, but the design should say that topic'd requests fall back gracefully and that `-By topic` will be empty. Note.

Another defect: the score is computed from ratings across ALL tasks of the repository — meaning the ranking is repository-global, but the ledger ratings are stored per task. Cross-task aggregation requires reading every `findings.json` in the repo on every panel run: how expensive? Let me measure: total size of .collab findings.json files.

Also the "90 days" window needs a timestamp source: rating.when (recorded at rating time) vs ledger when. And note ratings have no `topics`.

12. `-Require` and exit 5: check the existing exit codes to see whether 5 is already taken. Let me grep.

13. The availability line: "names only what is OUT, per roster entry (not per provider label)". Currently the hook line lists provider rows (`$r.name`), one per provider *label* from the config, plus roster info via `roster_selected`/`roster_position`. So a per-entry view needs codex-providers.ps1 -Json to emit per-entry rows. Let me check what codex-providers.ps1 -Json emits: does it have per-roster-entry rows with `roster_position`? From the hook code: `@($rows | Where-Object { $null -ne $_.roster_position })` — so rows are per provider, and some carry a roster_position. Let me read codex-providers.ps1.

Also: the hook line must stay ONE line and is added to context; with 11 entries and reset times, the "out" list can be long. And the hook runs `codex-providers.ps1 -Json -NoNetwork` — the reset time comes from ledger endpoint health, which is read from THIS repo's ledgers only. If the operator starts a session in a DIFFERENT repository, the health data is absent → the hook cannot know who is out. That's a real limitation for the addendum: "some topics should not be started without a particular reviewer" — but the availability knowledge is per-repository (CollabDir). Let me verify: `-CollabDir $CollabDir` with default '.collab' resolved against the git repo root of the current directory. Yes — per repo. So the hook line in another project says "all 11 reviewers available" even when Astra is out on a limit recorded in this repo. That's a significant defect for the addendum's purpose (the operator acting on it). Worth a finding.

Also: `9 of 11 reviewers available` counts roster entries; but an entry may be "not checked (launcher present)" under -NoNetwork (engine sign-in not checked) — is that "available"? The current hook prints 'not checked (launcher present)'. The new "N of M available" line must classify 'unknown' — the design doesn't say. Defect: unknown ≠ available; counting it as available would repeat exactly the mistake the addendum complains about (BytePlus 429 reported as available).

Critical: `$panelId = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString()` is generated at line 1237 — AFTER `Select-PanelMembers` at line 1221. So if the seed is "the panel id", the seed must be generated before selection, or the selection must move after. That's a re-ordering requirement the design doesn't mention — minor but concrete. More importantly: `[guid]::NewGuid()` is NOT derived from anything, so the seed is a random GUID → seeding from a random GUID means the draw is NOT reproducible from any inputs; reproducibility comes only from the recorded seed. That's fine if the seed is recorded (design says it is). But then the test "the seeded draw is reproducible (same seed -> same pick)" requires the seed to be injectable — the design gives no `-Seed`/test hook parameter, and there's no env test hook named. Tests are "fakes only" — how does a test control the seed? It must read the recorded seed from the dry-run output and re-run with the same eligible list, but the eligible list depends on live preflight. There IS a `-SkipPreflight` switch and `CODEX_CONSULT_TEST_*` env hooks (e.g. `CODEX_CONSULT_TEST_PANEL_GUARD_SEC`). And `Get-ConsultClock -Peek` for freezing time. So a test needs a new hook to inject the seed (e.g. `CODEX_CONSULT_TEST_PANEL_SEED`). The design's test list doesn't mention it → an unimplementable test as specified. Good finding.

Also important: `-DryRun` — does the dry run generate a panelId and thus a different seed than the real run? Yes: each invocation generates a fresh GUID, so the dry run's `routing.seed` ≠ the real run's seed → the dry run cannot predict the pick. The design says "the dry run prints the same" (the same routing object) — but with a per-run GUID seed, "the same" is impossible: the dry run prints A, the real run draws B. That's a real defect: the dry run's promise. Fix: derive the seed deterministically from stable inputs (task + purpose + brief hash + eligible lineages + a per-day/nonce counter) or let the dry run's seed be re-used via an explicit `-Seed`/`-PanelSeed` that the real run accepts. Actually the cleanest: `-PanelSeed <n>` optional, and dry run prints the seed; the operator can pass it to the real run. Or: dry run does not print `picked` at all.

Now I have a rich set of concrete test-breakage facts:
- `tests/harness-panel.ps1:339` asserts "3 of 3 roster entries would run, at once" — with a per-purpose default size (e.g. framing 3, checkpoint 1) these dry-run assertions change. Many tests use `-Panel` with `-Purpose` values; e.g. harness-roster.ps1:696-700 (weighty), 725 (chore), 613 ("2 of 3 entries ran"). With R14 default sizes, `-Panel -Purpose chore` (no default given!) and `-Panel -Purpose diff-review` (default 2) would change the counts and break these tests. The design's test list does not mention updating the existing panel/weighty/dry-run assertions → a defect in the "tests" section.

Let me check how many existing tests would break: any test asserting "N of M roster entries would run" with a purpose set. Let me count quickly the checks with `-Purpose` + `-Panel`.

Also, the harness's `Consult` helper and `Check` function — the tests are in `tests/harness-*.ps1` run by `tests/run-all.ps1`.

Now, another important defect: the panel's *numbers* (n, NN, handoff filenames) are assigned by position k in `$panelRunners` order (line 1288, 1299). If the draw reorders members, the handoff filenames (`NN-codex-<ReplyName>-<provider>.md`) are still per-provider so no collision. But `Get-PanelIgnorePrefixes` uses `$SiblingNns` — fine. And the ledger is "sorted by n in roster order" (harness-panel.ps1:367 asserts it). With a draw, the n order = picked order, so "the ledger sorted by n" no longer equals roster order — that assertion and the console "every member's output in roster order" (line 370) must be redefined as "picked order". Concrete test/behaviour defect.

Another: `$panelNumbers.Nn + $k - 1` — fine.

Another significant one: the `slot.ReplyName = "$ReplyName-$slug"` where slug = provider label lowercased. With byteplus having THREE entries, if a size-k panel picks two byteplus entries (deepseek + dola), the reply files are both `NN-codex-<ReplyName>-byteplus.md` — but NN differs per slot, so no collision. OK. But wait — with the current all-available panel, two byteplus members already coexist, so that's fine.

Hmm, but there IS a collision risk with `-Roles`: no.

Let me now check the "diversity" interaction with `Get-PanelPlan`: if the draw picks two entries of one endpoint group (byteplus limit 3) the concurrency plan handles it. Fine.

Now let me think about what else the design misses:

A. **Peak-hour / -OffPeakOnly**: `Get-PreflightVerdict` doesn't cover peak; the peak check is separate (`Get-PeakStatusNow`). `Select-PanelMembers` does NOT take peak into account (the brief says "availability (preflight, endpoint health, peak)" — let me verify: Select-PanelMembers' signature has no peak parameter; the peak check happens elsewhere in codex-consult.ps1 and applies to the run as a whole). So the brief's "code facts" line is slightly wrong: peak is not part of Select-PanelMembers. Minor, but relevant because with a size limit, the peak refusal is per-run, not per-member.

Let me verify: grep for 'Peak' in Select-PanelMembers region — the signature at 4889 has no peak. Confirmed. And the peak check in codex-consult.ps1 — let me see if it's per-member. Actually for a panel, the child members run with -PanelSpec; the peak check is "checked early and again immediately before launch - the launch-time result governs" (R7). With `-OffPeakOnly` and a panel, each member checks at launch → some members could be refused while others run. Not directly a design defect but worth a note: sizing counts members that WILL RUN at selection time, but a member can still be refused at launch (peak, launcher missing, pending record) → the actual count can be < k, with no top-up.

B. **The 90-day window and `Read-AllTaskConsults`**: the design says ratings are joined to the ledger by n. But `Read-AllTaskConsults` returns consults from ALL tasks flattened — and `n` is unique only WITHIN a task! So joining a rating (which lives in task T's findings.json, with `n` relative to T) to a consult requires the TASK as part of the key. If an implementer uses `Read-AllTaskConsults` (which drops the task) and joins by n, ratings from task A would attach to consultations of task B with the same n. THIS IS A REAL BLOCKER-CLASS DEFECT: the rating record itself carries `n`, `consult_id`, `lineage`, `provider`, `model`, `purpose` — `consult_id` is a GUID and is globally unique, so the safe join is by `consult_id`, not by `n`. But the design says "joined to the ledger entry by n". Note that `codex-findings.ps1 -Stats` joins findings to consults by `source.consult = n` **in the same task** (documented). And the rating record has `consult_id` copied — so a cross-task join must use consult_id. Also `Read-AllTaskConsults` does not return the task directory, so the join key must come from the rating's own fields (provider/model/purpose/consult_id) — the design's parenthetical ("Read-AllTaskConsults reads every ledger already") invites exactly the wrong join. Strong finding.

Additionally: the rating's `lineage`/`provider`/`model` are already denormalised into the rating record, so the join is unnecessary — the score can be computed from `ratings[]` alone. But then a rating whose ledger entry was a legacy entry says lineage 'unknown provenance' with empty provider/model → unusable for ranking (dropped silently). And a rating for a reviewer NOT in the roster (a `-Provider` run outside the roster) is also dropped. Fine but should be documented.

C. **Where does the score get computed?** In the bridge at panel time. It must read every task's findings.json (large: 87 KB CHANGELOG aside, findings.json files are ~4000 lines). Let me measure total bytes of all findings.json to quantify the cost. This is a per-panel-run cost added to a path that currently reads only sessions.json (Read-AllTaskConsults). Worth a note with a number.

D. **Concurrency/locking**: reading findings.json of all tasks while another task's panel is running — `Read-SharedText` handles sharing. OK.

E. **`-Topic`**: "a rating counts for the topics of its consultation" — but the rating record has no topics; topics live in the ledger entry (`topics[]`). So a topic'd score requires the join by consult_id after all (to get the topics), OR the rating record must copy `topics` at rating time (like it copies purpose). The design says "a rating counts for the topics of its consultation" without saying where the topics come from at score time → must be denormalised into the rating record (a schema change to `-Rate`) or joined via consult_id to the ledger. Defect: unspecified, and `-Rate` records written BEFORE R15 have no topics → all pre-R15 ratings are topic-less (acceptable, but must be stated).

F. **`-Rate` re-rating replaces** → the 90-day window on `rating.when` is the *rating* time, not the consultation time; re-rating refreshes it. So "ratings of the last 90 days" can include consultations from a year ago (rated yesterday) and exclude consultations from 91 days ago that were rated at the time. Which is intended? Probably consultation time is the better signal (a model's quality drifts with model versions, not with when the judge got round to rating). And model *renames* (glm-5.3 → glm-5.4) break the lineage key entirely: ratings for the old model never count for the new one — a cold start on every model bump, which for a fast-moving roster (the live roster shows gpt-6-astra, glm-5.3, kimi-k2.5, qwen3.8-max) means the score is permanently sparse. Strong argument for Q1 (confidence prior) and for keying by lab/model-family rather than exact model id. This is a genuinely valuable framing challenge: **the roster's identity churns faster than 90 days of ratings accumulate**, so any per-model ranking is mostly neutral-1 + noise; the ranking signal should probably be per LAB (family) with a per-model correction, or the design should accept that it will rarely have data.

Let me verify the model-version churn claim from the ledgers: check distinct lineages recorded over time in this repo (e.g. gpt-5.1 → gpt-6-astra). From the example roster: `openai :: gpt-5.1` (examples/) vs live `openai :: gpt-6-astra`. And the ledger sample shows `gemini :: gemini-3.8-flash-high`. Let me quickly list distinct lineages across all ledgers to demonstrate churn + sparsity. That's cheap and gives hard numbers for the answer.

G. **Exploration vs. the weighty gate**: exploration "uniformly from the eligible rest" — eligible = passed availability AND the weighty gate? Presumably yes. Must be stated; otherwise exploration could pull a weighty reviewer onto a light purpose, defeating the gate (a token-cost bug).

H. **`-PanelSize` vs `-PanelAll` vs `-PanelSize` > eligible**: if k > eligible count, run all eligible (fine) but must be stated; and `-PanelSize 0`/negative → refuse.

I. **`-Require` on a single run with `-Provider`**: `-Provider` already fixes the reviewer; `-Require` is then redundant except for the *reset-time message*. Also `-Require <lineage>` naming: lineage is '<provider> :: <model>' (with ' [engine]'), but a roster entry may have no model (resolves from config) — so `-Require 'openai'` vs `-Require 'openai :: gpt-6-astra'`: which forms are accepted? The addendum's roster `require` example uses `"openai :: gpt-6-astra"` (a lineage string). Matching must be by lineage string comparison — but `Format-ReviewerLineage` adds ' [agy]' for engines, and the ledger's `lineage` field... let me check whether the ledger stores `lineage` with the engine suffix. From harness-roster: "-Rate records lineage '... [agy]'". So yes. So `-Require 'gemini :: gemini-3.1-pro-high'` would NOT match the entry's lineage string 'gemini :: gemini-3.1-pro-high [agy]'. Concrete usability defect: the require key must accept both forms or the roster-position form. Good finding.

J. **`-Require` + the panel's own skip semantics**: today an unavailable entry is skipped and the run proceeds. `-Require` turns that into a refusal BEFORE anything starts — but the availability check itself is time-dependent and per-endpoint: `Get-PreflightVerdict` with `-RosterWalk` marks a quota-without-reset as unavailable, whereas WITHOUT `-RosterWalk` (a single `-Provider` run) the same endpoint is AVAILABLE with a warning (line 4795: `elseif ($RosterWalk -and $Health -and $Health.Quota)`). So `-Require X` on a single `-Provider X` run would use which mode? If it uses the non-roster-walk verdict, a required reviewer that hit a limit 10 minutes ago reads "available" and the run starts and fails; if it uses the roster-walk verdict, `-Require` refuses where today's single run would proceed with a warning. The design must pick, and it changes existing behaviour. Strong finding (the `-RosterWalk` flag is the exact code location: codex-consult-common.ps1:4795).

K. **The hook line and `-NoNetwork`**: the addendum's example says `gemini :: * (until Sun 21:30)` — a wildcard for the model, i.e. per ENDPOINT. That contradicts item 9's "per roster entry (not per provider label)" in the same sentence. The example itself admits the endpoint granularity for engines. Good catch — internal inconsistency in the addendum.

L. **Counting "N of M available"**: with `-NoNetwork`, an agy row is `unknown` ('not checked (launcher present)') unless a usable reply in the last 60 min evidences the sign-in. Is `unknown` counted as available? Today the hook prints it distinctly. The new count would either overstate availability (counting unknown as available — the exact error the addendum complains about) or print "9 of 11 available, 1 not checked". Unspecified → defect.

M. **One line, 11 entries**: the hook line goes into the agent's context at EVERY session start. Truncation at 60 chars per reason (codex-consult-hook.ps1:78) would cut "until Sun 20:35, 2d 10h" style text. Also the SessionStart hook has a 30 s timeout (README:241) and costs ~1 s today; adding per-entry resolution (11 identity resolutions + 11 preflight verdicts, each possibly running `codex login status`) could push the cost up. Let me check: does the providers walk run `codex login status` once (LoginCache) — yes, `-LoginCache @{}` is shared. OK, cost is bounded. But `Select-RosterReviewer` already walks all entries; the new per-entry view needs the full walk's per-entry verdicts, which `Select-RosterReviewer` does compute but discards (it returns only Skipped + the selected Entry). Note: `Skipped` stops accumulating once a winner is found! Look at Select-RosterReviewer: it returns as soon as it finds an available entry — so entries AFTER the first available one are never checked. So a "who is out" line built on `Select-RosterReviewer`'s Skipped list would MISS every unavailable entry that sits after the first available one. That's a concrete, verifiable defect: the walk short-circuits at codex-consult-common.ps1:4856-4859 (`return $r` on the first available). To name every entry that is OUT, you need the full non-short-circuiting walk — which is `Select-PanelMembers` (it walks all). So `codex-providers.ps1 -Short` should be built on Select-PanelMembers-like logic, not on the walk. Excellent finding, code-verified.

Also note `Select-PanelMembers` does not accept `-NoNetwork` (its signature at 4889 has no NoNetwork param!) whereas `Select-RosterReviewer` does (4830). So building the hook's per-entry line on Select-PanelMembers would perform the agy network sign-in check (`agy models`) at every session start — a network call in a hook documented as "No network call" and bounded to ~1 s. Concrete defect: `-NoNetwork` is missing from Select-PanelMembers' parameter list (codex-consult-common.ps1:4889). Verified. And `Get-PreflightVerdict` at 4907 is called WITHOUT `-NoNetwork`. That's a great finding.

N. **R14 size vs. the weighty gate ordering**: "The size counts members that will RUN" — the weighty gate is applied per entry inside the walk (line 4910). So eligible = available AND (not weighty OR purpose weighty OR -All). Fine, but the design must say the size applies AFTER the gate. Minor.

O. **`lab` and `parallel`/endpoint groups**: the design's `lab` is free text and defaults to the provider label. But the concurrency plan already has a *better* notion of grouping (endpoint fingerprint). Two different concepts (lab = who trained it; endpoint = who serves/quota) that both default to the provider label will be confused. Recommend: `lab` should default to nothing (absent = no diversity constraint) or be validated against a known list; and the diversity pass should be explicit that it can pick 2 members of ONE endpoint (running serially, doubling the wall clock) — with byteplus parallel=3 they'd run at once, but for a label without `parallel`, diversity across labs could still concentrate on one endpoint. Actually the opposite: diversity spreads labs, which usually spreads endpoints. Fine.

P. **The seeded draw and `-PanelOrder roster` and single runs**: item 7 says single runs are unchanged. Good. But `codex-providers.ps1`'s "roster -> would select X" line and the hook's would then disagree with what a `-Panel` picks. Minor: the availability line should not imply the panel's composition.

Q. **Determinism/reproducibility of the draw across PS versions**: `[System.Random]::new(seed)` — .NET Framework 4.x vs .NET 6+: seeded Random uses the same Knuth subtractive algorithm in both (documented stable for the seeded ctor). But `Random.NextDouble()`-based weighted draws accumulate floating point differently? No, same. The bigger risk is that the design doesn't pin the ALGORITHM (weighted draw without replacement: which method — cumulative + NextDouble, or Efraimidis-Spirakis keys?). Without pinning it, "the seeded draw is reproducible" only holds within one implementation. And the repo runs on BOTH PS 5.1 and PS 7 (hook docstring). Recommend: derive the permutation from SHA-256 (`Get-Sha256Hex` exists) so it is byte-identical across runtimes — a concrete, code-grounded remedy.

R. **Findings/telemetry feedback loop**: the score is computed from ratings the coordinator enters by hand (`-Rate`). If the score drives selection, the operator's ratings now control who gets consulted → a self-reinforcing loop: a reviewer that is rarely picked gets no new ratings, its score ages out of the 90-day window and falls back to neutral 1 (or its all-purpose score), which then gets it picked again. Actually that's self-correcting via the neutral fallback. But there's a subtle bug: "a lineage with no ratings on this purpose scores its all-purpose score, else the neutral 1" — read literally: no purpose ratings → use all-purpose; no ratings at all → neutral 1. Fine. But when the 90-day window expires, the all-purpose score is also computed over 90 days → also empty → neutral 1. So an idle reviewer decays to neutral, which is HIGHER than a well-rated reviewer with one 'no' (0.25) — i.e. **an unreviewed newcomer outranks a proven reviewer that once disappointed**. With floor 0.25 vs neutral 1.0, one 'no' rating is a 4x penalty that lasts 90 days. That's the strongest argument for Q1's rate+prior. Concrete: score for [1 no] = max(0.25, 1-1) = 0.25; for [10 yes, 1 no] = 1+10-1 = 10; for [no ratings] = 1. So a single 'no' with no other ratings = 0.25 < 1 = never rated. Verified arithmetic from the formula in the brief.

Also: score can be huge (1 + sum(yes)) → weights are unbounded, so one lineage with 30 ratings dominates the draw (weight 31 vs 1) → the panel becomes effectively deterministic towards the most-rated reviewer, and exploration is the only source of variety. With weights 31:10:1:0.25 the draw picks the top one ~73% of the time. So "weighted draw" + additive score ≈ "always pick the best-rated", which contradicts the intent of ranking-by-track-record-with-exploration. A rate-based score in [0,1] with a prior keeps weights comparable. Strong answer to Q1.

S. **Q3 (diversity before rank)**: the regret case is concrete from the live roster: default lab = provider label → 'byteplus' is ONE lab, so the diversity pass takes the best-ranked of {deepseek-v4.1-flash, dola-seed-2.0-pro, kimi-k2.5} and then fills by rank; meanwhile 'kimi' (k3, actually Moonshot) is a SEPARATE lab and gets its own slot. So for k=2 the panel could be {byteplus's best, kimi :: k3} = two Moonshot-family models while DeepSeek and ByteDance are excluded — the exact opposite of diversity. Verified from the live roster + config base_urls.

Also: with 11 entries and ~7 distinct real labs, a framing panel of 3 spends all three slots on lab representatives, so rank barely matters and the *best* reviewer may be excluded (Astra is 'weighty' and only joins weighty purposes — framing IS weighty, ok).

T. **The design floor (item 3)**: "-Panel on those purposes warns when fewer than 2 members will run" — but the default size for framing is 3, so the warning fires when availability collapses; the warning is post-hoc (after selection, before launch) — with `-DryRun` it prints. But a *warning* (not a refusal) contradicts item 11 of the addendum ("never silently proceeds" + ask the operator). A warning in a non-interactive bridge run IS silent proceeding: the bridge cannot ask. So the floor rule belongs in the skill (as item 11 says) and the bridge's warning is only a hint. Also note: the bridge runs non-interactively from the coordinator; a `Write-Host` warning is only seen if the coordinator reads stdout. Worth a note: make it a `runWarnings` entry (there's an existing `$runWarnings` mechanism at codex-consult.ps1 — I saw `foreach ($rw in $runWarnings) { Write-Host "WARNING: ..." }`). Good: the remedy is to add it to $runWarnings so it lands in the ledger/summary consistently. Let me verify $runWarnings is recorded in the ledger. Quick grep.

U. **R16 `-Role` and prompt hash/thread reuse**: does the bridge reuse a parent thread for the same lineage? Yes (`Select-ParentThread` by lineage). A role'd consultation resuming a thread that was created without the role is fine (prompt-only). But `fork`/`resume` means the reviewer sees its own earlier unrole'd answer — acceptable. Note only.

V. **`-Roles a,b,c` count vs picked count**: "assigns roles in order to the picked members (the rest: none)" — if there are more roles than members, the extra roles are silently ignored? Should refuse. And with the draw, order is random (see above).

Let me do a couple of final verifications:
1. distinct lineages across ledgers (churn + sparsity numbers), total ratings count, and total size of findings.json files.
2. `$runWarnings` recorded in the ledger?
3. whether the ledger has a `topics`-like field already / and `lineage` field.

Then write the answer. Let me be efficient — two commands.
